why: A Run id rendered as ONE path segment and ONE SQL identifier. It is the first half of a temp Dataset's storage name (ADR 0028) — `tmp_<slug>_<hex8>` — and it has THREE writers: `_slug` in the Python SDK, `tempSlug` in the Go SDK, and `safeName` in the orchestrator, which sanitises the name again on its way to a DuckLake table and an object key. The two SDKs must agree byte for byte; the orchestrator must leave what they produce ALONE, because a name a caller reads in `kontra dataset ls` and a name the lake stores being two strings for one Dataset is the drift a run-derived name exists to remove.
measured: 2026-08-28. The three rules are NOT the same rule, which both SDK comments said they were. (1) BOUND: the SDKs cut at 64; `safeName` does not truncate. (2) EMPTY: the SDKs fall back to `run`, `safeName` to `unnamed`. (3) LEADING DIGIT: `safeName` prefixes `a` so the name is a legal bare SQL identifier; neither SDK does — see the `2026-sweep` row, whose `safe_name` is `a2026-sweep`. And on RAW input the character mapping itself differs: `safeName`'s regex has no `u` flag, so it walks UTF-16 code units and turns one astral code point into TWO underscores where both SDKs write one. None of that is live, and the reason is the composed shape: the orchestrator is only ever handed `tmp_<slug>_<hex8>`, which is already ASCII, already under any bound that matters, and always starts with `t`. That is the bound on this corpus, stated so the next reader does not have to re-derive it: what is pinned is that the SDKs agree and that the orchestrator is a no-op on their output.

cases.why: a real Run id — `<type>-<unixseconds>`, which must pass through untouched
an explicit --id carrying a path separator and a colon: the two characters an object key and a SQL identifier cannot hold
a quote and a semicolon — the injection shape, because this string becomes a table name
a dot and a dash, which are LEGAL and must SURVIVE; the class most likely to be over-sanitised
non-ASCII letters: Python's str.isalnum() is Unicode-aware, so the isascii() guard is the whole reason these are underscores rather than letters
an astral code point — ONE rune to Python and Go, TWO UTF-16 code units to a browser
a combining sequence: two code points that render as one glyph, so the count differs from the glyph count on every side
longer than the bound, which must be cut to exactly 64
one past the bound — the off-by-one a `>=` and a `>` disagree on
empty: an id nothing can be derived from still has to yield a legal segment
nothing but illegal characters, so the empty-fallback must NOT fire — `___` is a legal name
a LEADING DIGIT, which is legal in a path segment and not in a bare SQL identifier: the one row where the SDKs and the orchestrator part company
a NUL and a newline — the two bytes that silently end a string somewhere downstream
